items.title: Recalled
items.reason: Across its 99-minute South Korean psychological mystery, Soo-jin wakes with amnesia after an apparent accident and experiences disturbing visions that seem to predict dangers to other people. Her apparent husband Ji-hoon restricts what she knows, tracks her movements and presses plans to move to Canada, creating immediate uncertainty about whether the visions are supernatural, unreliable or buried memories. Meaningful information arrives in successive portions of the film: an apparently accurate vision of a child's road accident, a construction-site police inquiry and CCTV implicating Ji-hoon, a former colleague's account of Soo-jin's troubled marriage, photographs of an unfamiliar man and fragments of an earlier fall. Later disclosures identify the supposed husband as her protective adoptive brother, distinguish him from her actual husband and explain the violent events preceding her memory loss; the supposed premonitions are reinterpreted through recovered memories. Forbes and Cinema Escapist specifically describe rapidly paced revisions to the viewer's understanding, while the longer review at MIB details intermediate evidence rather than only a final twist. The counterweight is that the scenario uses familiar amnesia and domestic-abuse tropes and is less demanding as a clue puzzle than its sustained reversals imply. It is primarily an unreliable-perspective mystery and tense identity deception, not a conventional police procedural or a technology-driven conspiracy; intermittent construction-site peril is not nonstop action.

items.title: The Absent One
items.reason: The 119-minute Danish Department Q mystery reopens the 1994 murders of twins after their father leaves a case file for detective Carl Morck. The original conviction appears suspicious: a working-class suspect received an unusually light sentence and elite legal representation, while an old emergency call and photographs connect wealthy former boarding-school students to a missing witness, Kimmie. The parallel flashbacks disclose aspects of the original violence before investigators can prove them, so the suspense partly concerns catching and protecting people rather than guessing the killers. Further consequential findings span the middle and late story: hospital records illuminate Kimmie's disappearance, the police commissioner's school ties explain leaks to the suspects, and a disclosure about trophies kept by one suspect directs detectives to physical evidence. The inquiry becomes a race to reach the witness before the powerful former students and their hired pursuer do. The Guardian explicitly praises clues and revelations throughout, while Time Out notes that the villains are easy to suspect early, and Rotten Tomatoes' collected criticism points to formulaic genre devices and an overwrought climax. Thus the cold-case investigation and recurring evidence are strong, but the revelation cadence is lower than a wholly unpredictable whodunit and the action is episodic. The shadowy, polished cinematography is distinct from its familiar Nordic-noir visual styling; the plot's police insider and elite cover-up support real corruption without a vast geopolitical conspiracy.
